question.problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}$ at the point where $x=-1$ is{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (6x+2) \\  & =\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=-1} \\  & =\frac{6(-1)+2}{2\sqrt{3(-1)^{2}+2(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$
